# Characterization of Radiation-Induced Errors in Superconducting Qubits Protected with Various Gap-Engineering Strategies

Impacts from high-energy particles cause correlated errors in superconducting qubits by increasing the quasiparticle density in the vicinity of the Josephson junctions (JJs). Such errors are particularly harmful as they cannot be easily remedied via conventional error correcting codes. Recent experiments reduced correlated errors by making the difference in superconducting gap energy across the JJ larger than the qubit transition energy. In this work, we assess gap engineering near the JJ (δ∆JJ) and the capacitor/ground-plane (δ∆M1) by exposing arrays of transmon qubits to two sources of radiation. For α-particles from an 241Am source, we observe T1 errors correlated in space and time, supporting a hypothesis that hadronic cosmic rays are a major contributor to the 10−10 error floor observed in Ref. 1. For electrons from a pulsed linear accelerator, we observe temporally correlated T1 and T2 errors, this measurement is insensitive to spatial correlations. We observe that the severity of correlated T1 errors is reduced for qubit arrays with a greater degree of gap engineering at the JJ. For both T1 and T2 errors, the recovery time is hastened by an increased δ∆M1, which we attribute to the trapping of quasiparticles into the capacitor/ground-plane. We construct a model of quasiparticle dynamics that qualitatively agrees with our observations. This work reinforces the multifaceted influence of radiation on superconducting qubits and provides strategies for improving

Interactions of environmental radiation with the substrate of superconducting circuits are a source of nonequilibrium material excitations. These interactions generate phonons by (1) creating electron-hole pairs that can recombine into phonons and (2) direct nuclear displacement. In turn, these phonons can interact with superconducting materials to create Bogoliubov quasiparticles (QPs). This mechanism is widely leveraged as a radiation-detection technique [2, 3] and has been identified as a source of correlated errors in superconducting

The effects of radiation on qubits are correlated in both space and time [1, 5, 12, 14, 15], introducing qubit frequency shifts and state transition errors that are difficult to rectify within standard quantum error correction (QEC) frameworks [1, 12, 16]. While QEC schemes are being developed to accommodate correlated errors [16– 19], they come at the cost of increased resource requirements. Device-level mitigation strategies could reduce

the occurrence, extent, and severity of such correlated errors — and thereby the associated resource overhead. One strategy for device-level mitigation of relaxation errors is by engineering the superconducting gap in the vicinity of the Josephson junction (JJ) [11, 12, 20–22]. In qubits with Al/AlOx/Al JJs this can be achieved by tuning the thickness of the Al layers comprising the JJ [23]. If the gap difference across the JJ (δ∆JJ) is greater than the qubit energy (hfqb), QPs thermalized to the gap edge will not be able to facilitate relaxation errors by absorbing a qubit photon and tunneling in one direction. We refer to this as “JJ gap-engineering” (JJ GE). Previous work has used this technique to make qubits insensitive to the higher-rate, lower-energy (below 1 MeV deposited) portion of the natural radiation spectrum [21], which consists primarily of γ-rays from trace radioactive elements and cosmic ray leptons (electrons and muons) [24, 25]. Despite the progress of JJ GE and other mitigation strategies [11–13, 15, 26–31], a residual source of correlated errors (approximately one-per-hour) apparently remains a limiting factor in state-of-the-art, belowthreshold QEC [1, 12, 32]. This rate is consistent with what would be expected from the higher-energy (above 1 MeV deposited) portion of the natural radiation specarXiv:2603.13460v2 [quant-ph] 24 Mar 2026

trum, which consists primarily of cosmic-ray hadrons (protons and neutrons) [24, 25]. These hadronic cosmic rays could be expected to overcome the protection of JJ GE due to the order-of-magnitude greater energy deposited in the qubit substrate. Potential sensitivity to these energies, which can also be reached by terrestrial α-particles impinging on the chip, would not have been readily discerned in previous work due to the short duration (100 min) of the experiment [21]. Our work has three main goals: (1) to investigate whether these hadronic comic rays can explain the residual correlated error rate observed [1], (2) to study the potential limits of JJ GE, and (3) to quantify the effect of a superconducting gap difference between the metal forming the JJ and the metal forming the capacitor/groundplane. We refer to the superconducting gap difference at this interface as δ∆M1. To this end we designed and fabricated arrays of transmon qubits with three superconducting gap profiles and exposed them to two distinct types of radiation: 5.5 MeV α-particles from 241Am and 10 MeV to 20 MeV electrons (e−) from a linear accelerator (linac) at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) Controlled Linac Irradiation of Quantum

The measurements with 241Am described in Sec. III serve two purposes. Primarily they address goal 1, informing whether low-rate, high-energy cosmic ray hadrons can be a source of the correlated errors observed in recent QEC experiments [1, 24]. In addition, they directly enable us to study the effects of α-particle impacts on qubit substrates. These particles can be emitted by radioactive contaminants in materials that form the qubit package (e.g., ceramic interposer PCBs, connectors, and dust) [24, 25, 33, 34] or by radon emanated from qubit package materials [34], and are a well known and challenging background to mitigate in rare-event particle

Our measurements at CLIQUE, presented in Sec. IV, allow us to precisely investigate the influence of the superconducting gap profile on radiation response, addressing goals 2 and 3. These measurements leverage the facility’s two key advantages: triggered timing and tunable beam current. The timing and 10 Hz repetition rate of the electron beam trigger enabled the collection of datasets with O(1000) samples of e−-qubit interactions at a range of energies. These individual interactions are averaged to reduce sensitivity to non-radiation effects. We probed the energy dependence of qubit response by tuning the beam current of the linac. Throughout this work we measure radiation’s effect on qubit excitation and relaxation rates. Additionally, we employ pulse sequences tailored to detect transient qubit frequency shifts [12, 36]. We find that each quantity’s response to radiation is influenced, but not eliminated, by the qubit’s superconducting gap profile. We conclude by constructing a model connecting QP dynamics with qubit transition rates, and demonstrate that this model re-creates our key observations, Sec. V. II. QUBIT ARRAYS AND GAP PROFILES

This work focuses on three chips, each with ten individual transmons and nearly identical geometric designs. Each chip has a distinct superconducting gap profile, sketched to scale in Fig. 1(a). All layout features are identical to the array described in Ref. [7] with the exception of JJ lead thicknesses as described in Table I and Fig. 1. We refer to the three metal layers as M1, M2, and M3, ordered from lowest to highest superconducting gap [Fig. 1(a)]. Layers M1L and M1R are the base metalization and form the ground plane and qubit capacitor, with L and R indicating position relative to the JJ. Layers M2 and M3 form the JJ. The substrate of each array was a 5 mm × 5 mm × 350 μm silicon chip. The JJs on qubits in these arrays are distributed between two orientations: “slow,” (S) where the low gap side of the JJ contacts the relatively small, isolated qubit capacitor, and “fast,” (F) where the low gap side of the JJ contacts the relatively large ground plane [Fig. 1(d)]. In Ref. 7, this difference was shown to influence the qubit relaxation error recovery timescale. It was hypothesized that since relaxation errors are driven by the QP population in the relatively low gap M2 layer, the QP dynamics differ between the qubit capacitor and the ground plane. This was attributed to a difference in trapping efficiency, caused by the ground plane containing more features which can remove QPs from the system (e.g., lower-gap air bridges and galvanic contact to the normal metal of the qubit package). In this work, we use the difference in response between fast and slow JJ orientations to identify the influence of QP dynamics in layer M1 on

The three superconducting gap profiles studied are as follows. There are three relevant energy scales: the qubit energy hfqb and the two superconducting gap differences δ∆JJ = ∆M3 − ∆M2 and δ∆M1 = ∆M2 − ∆M1. For fabrication consistency, the thinnest M3 layer used was 10 nm, limiting the sum (δ∆JJ +δ∆M1)/h to be less than approximately 10 GHz. The No-JJ-GE array acts as a control and was fabricated at the same time as the chip studied in Ref. 7. There was no special care taken to mitigate correlated errors from environmental radiation, and so δ∆JJ was less than the qubit energy, and δ∆M1/h had a designed value of 0.2 GHz. The next array, JJ-Only, had the largest designed δ∆JJ/h at 10 GHz and the lowest designed δ∆M1/h at 0.1 GHz. This profile is in the style of those measured in Refs. 1, 12, and 21. The final array, JJ&M1, also has a nominal δ∆JJ greater than the qubit energy. Additionally, a nominal δ∆M1/h of approximately 3 GHz was introduced to test the efficacy of using layer M1 as a QP trap. This large δ∆M1 limits the magnitude of δ∆JJ on this array to a designed value of 7 GHz. Table I contains the nominal gap engineering parameters, estimated from transition temperature measurements on films from the same fabrication process, as well as measured average qubit frequencies.

As the no-JJ-GE array was thoroughly characterized in Refs. 7 and 36, we focus our discussion on the two arrays designed with δ∆JJ > hfqb. Typical energy relaxation times T1 for the qubits under study were greater than 25 μs (see Table II in Appendix A 3 for further details). Throughout, we refer to the qubit ground state as |0⟩ and the ith excited state as |i⟩. Unless otherwise stated, time refers to the time since a particle-qubit interaction. III. QUBIT RESPONSE TO α-PARTICLES

Sensitivity to high-energy particles, such as α-particles and hadronic cosmic rays, was tested using a 37 kBq 241Am source inside of a dilution refrigerator at MIT. This source emits both 5.5 MeV α-particles and 59 keV γ-rays. The source was glued to a copper mount approximately 3 cm away from the qubit substrate surface and faced the side with the qubits. When measuring the JJ-Only array, the source was collimated using an approximately 100 μm diameter pinhole in copper tape, and when measuring the JJ&M1 array, the source was collimated using an 7.96 mm thick custom machined block of Cu101 with three 180 μm diameter holes. Both collimators were designed such that the α-particle impact rate was approximately 0.077 s−1. An illustration of this setup is shown in Fig. 10 of Appendix A 2. The data acquisition is similar to what is described in Refs. 4 and

B. Data Collection and Analysis Three datasets were collected with each array, each using a unique measurement sequence [Fig. 2]: (A) a measurement primarily sensitive to qubit relaxation, (B) a measurement primarily sensitive to qubit excitation, and (C) a measurement sequence that alternates between these two. Appendix A 1 contains additional details about the measurement sequences. Sequence A comprised a repeated sequence of an Xπ (a rotation of π radians around the X-axis of the Bloch sphere), a 1 μs delay, and a 4 μs readout. The measurement uses “heralding”, meaning the previous cycle’s measurement was used to determine whether a qubit relaxation occurred, defined to be whenever the qubit was measured in |0⟩ twice in a

Measured in |0⟩ → no Xπ → Measure in |1⟩. (2) Sequence C alternates whether the Xπ is applied, allowing for identification of qubit relaxations on measurements bracketing an Xπ [condition 1] and excitation on measurements not bracketing an Xπ [condition 2]. An aspect of these sequences is that the qubit trajectory is ambiguous following an excited-state measurement. For example, in the qubit relaxation sequence (A), measuring |1⟩ → |0⟩ could be due to two relaxation errors (relaxation both before and after the Xπ ), or no relaxation errors (the Xπ caused the state transition). We remove such cases from our analysis. Each dataset comprised 250 × 106 measurement cycles. The cycle duration was 6.95 μs, resulting in a dataset with approximately 29 min of live time. Increases in qubit relaxation rates due to radiation were identified using the same matched filter procedure as was used in Ref. 7 (see Supplementary Note 1 therein) except using a 100 μs decaying exponential as the filter template (cf., a 5 ms decaying exponential that integrated to 0). As the change in qubit excitation rate due to radiation is a smaller signal relative to the relaxation rate, identifying them with sequence B (primarily sensitive to qubit excitations) was inefficient. To mitigate this type of signal-to-noise ratio issue, we instead identified qubit excitations using sequence C: a matched filter is used to identify radiation impacts from increases in the qubit relaxation rate with measurements that bracket an Xπ , and qubit excitations for those same radiation impacts are studied with measurements that do not bracket an Xπ . Details on identifying radiation impacts are presented in Appendix B.

We display results from these datasets in Fig. 3. Panels (a) and (b) use sequence A, while (c) and (d) use sequence C. The JJ-Only array is shown in all panels while the JJ&M1 array is only shown in Fig. 3(b) — the fast recovery timescale of the JJ&M1 array resulted in a lower trigger efficiency for sequence C relative to sequence A. Despite strong protection at the JJ, δ∆JJ > hfqb, we observe an increase in the rate of correlated qubit errors with respect to background in both arrays [Fig. 3(a, b)]. These correlated errors are created by transient increases in both the qubit relaxation and excitation rates [Fig. 3(c)]. The characteristic recovery timescale of these increased transition rates is approximately 100 μs, an order of magnitude faster than the No-JJ-GE array [7, 36], suggesting that a different mechanism mediates these transitions in JJ GE qubits. Figure 3(a) displays the largest observed event in the JJ-Only dataset, determined by the matched filter trigger. Figure 3(b) compares the correlated relaxation error rate integrated above various values for 241Am and background datasets for both arrays. The background datasets were collected on the same arrays in the same cryostat during a different cooldown with no radiation source present. Three of four datasets (the JJ-Only array with and without 241Am, and the JJ&M1 array without 241Am) included 9 qubits. The exception, the JJ&M1 array dataset with 241Am, includes 8 qubits — two qubits in this array had nearly identical frequencies during this cooldown (∆fqb <1 MHz), preventing them from being independently addressed by the Xπ pulse. The result of this estimation is shown in Fig. 3(d), where the qubit temperature is observed to transiently increase following the α-particle impact and return to equilibrium over the course of approximately 1 ms. This highlights that although the relaxation rate largely recovers in hundreds of μs, effects of radiation are present on the ms timescale. D. Implications for Future Processors While JJ GE significantly mitigates radiation-induced errors, qubit arrays protected in this way remain sensitive to radiation that deposits energy on the scale of a few MeV. This indicates a sensitivity to energy depositions comparable to that of the hadronic component (protons and neutrons) of the cosmic ray spectrum. We note that the 1-per-hour rate observed in Ref. 1 is consistent with the rate of cosmic rays above approximately 1 MeV, where the radiation spectrum is primarily hadronic [24]. Such hadronic cosmic rays can be mitigated by operation in shallow (approximately 15 m to 30 m) underground facilities, where cosmic ray protons are attenuated with a mass attenuation thickness of approximately 1.6 m.w.e. (meters of water equivalent) [25, 31, 38]. Additionally, it highlights the importance of removing sources of αparticle radiation (e.g., trace radioisotopes present in connectors and ceramics [25, 33]) to avoid such correlated errors. This observed sensitivity to 5.5 MeV α-particles motivates the development of further radiation mitigation strategies, discussed further in Section VI.

Precise measurements of qubit recovery dynamics and energy sensitivity were performed using CLIQUE [36]. This precision was facilitated by the accelerator’s ability to time-tag e−-qubit interactions and its trigger rate of 10 Hz, enabling us to rapidly collect and average together large samples of events. We varied the mean number of electrons incident on the qubit substrate from 0.1 e− to 6.9 e−. The accelerator current was monitored by an off-axis scintillator detector, correlated to electrons-ontarget by a dedicated measurement where the qubit package was replaced with an electron detector [36]. The accelerated electrons have energies from 10 MeV to 20 MeV and therefore are minimum ionizing [39], allowing the average number of electrons-on-target to be converted to the energy deposited in the substrate. The mean energy deposited was 145 keV/e− and the most probable energy deposited was 96 keV/e−. The details of this conversion are presented in Ref. 36. Using this conversion, the range of measured accelerator currents corresponds to an average of 14.5 keV to 1 MeV deposited in the qubit

We performed five measurement sequences at CLIQUE [36]. To estimate qubit transition rates, we used sequences A, B, and D from Fig. 2. Sequence D was used with two variants: with the conditional pulse set to prepare the qubit in |0⟩ (D|0⟩), and sequence D with the conditional pulse set to prepare the qubit in |1⟩ (D|1⟩). To measure transient qubit frequency shifts, we used a repeated Ramsey interferometry sequence [Fig. 6(a)]. Further information regarding this interferometry sequence is presented in Sec. IV C. The qubit arrays were measured sequentially, each in a dedicated cryostat cooldown. Within an array we measured up to nine qubits simultaneously. The measurements were broken into basic units of “runs.” Each run comprised 107 measurements and contained on the order of 103 accelerator triggers, totaling approximately 70 s of data, with the specific value dependent on the measurement sequence used. Appendix A 3 presents more details on the data collection process, with Fig. 11 showing the energy distribution of the data collected at CLIQUE.

B. Qubit Relaxation and Excitation We use measurement sequence D|1⟩ (D|0⟩) to estimate changes in the qubit relaxation (excitation) rate, estimated as the change in probability of measuring |0⟩ (|1⟩). In Fig. 4 we show the change in these state probabilities in response to electrons from CLIQUE as a function of the energy deposited in the qubit substrate. The energy bins are described in panel (a), we use panels (a-d) to show qubit relaxation, and panels (e-h) to show qubit excitation. Each energy bin is an average of approximately 5000 accelerator triggers. Panels (a), (b), (e), and (f) show the average change in state probability as a function of time. Panels (c) and (g) show the peak change in state probability. Panels (d) and (h) show the recovery time, as estimated from a decaying exponential fit to data in panels (a), (b), (e), and (f). We describe the details of the fit procedure in Appendix A 3. We hypothesize the exceptionally low recovery time reconstructed for the 14.5 keV to 145 keV JJ-Only array relaxation data is a fit to a noise fluctuation, due to the small signal size. As with the 241Am dataset, we observe a transient increase in qubit relaxation and excitation rate as a result of radiation depositing energy into the substrate. As expected, the change in rate is larger for greater energies deposited in the qubit substrate [Fig. 4(c, g)]. Beyond these confirmations, a more striking observation is that qubits are affected by the lowest accelerator current measured: an average of 0.1 e− to 1 e− impinging on the Si, equivalent to an average of 14.5 keV to 145 keV deposited. This indicates that the higher-rate (one per 101 s in Ref. 7), lower-energy radiation from cosmic ray muons and terrestrial γ-rays can still increase error probabilities in qubits strongly protected by JJ gap engineering. While radiation at these energy scales currently does not affect leading QEC experiments [1, 21], a sensitivity will likely become apparent as qubit T1 and T2 improve. Additionally, by comparing the JJ-Only and JJ&M1 arrays, we observe that the degree of JJ GE (δ∆JJ/hfqb) matters. Even though both arrays have δ∆JJ > hfqb, the JJ-Only array has a 3× lower peak change ground-state probability [Fig. 4(c)]. This is consistent with the qubit transitions being facilitated by hot QPs as suggested by the 241Am dataset — for the same QP energy distribution, more QPs satisfy the qubit relaxation condition of Eqn. 3 and so the observed rate is greater. A similar effect can be observed when measuring the excitation error rate [Fig. 4(g)]. The ratio of severity between the two gap profiles is different for excitation compared with relaxation. We hypothesize this is because the energy required to facilitate qubit transitions differs between relaxation and excitation (cf., Eqns. 3 - 5). A more quantitative discussion is presented in Section V. While the peak error rate is lower for the JJ-Only array, the radiation-induced transition rates remain elevated longer compared to the JJ&M1 array [Fig. 4(d, h)]. We hypothesize that this is because the larger δ∆M1 causes layer M1 to act as a QP trap, shortening the re-

Examining qubit relaxation for the JJ-Only array (low δ∆M1), we see a dramatic difference in response between the two orientations, an effect which can only be created by the influence of QPs in layer M1 (cf., QP dynamics solely in layers M2 and M3 should be agnostic to the JJ orientation). The difference in response between orientations is significantly reduced for qubits in the JJ&M1 array (high δ∆M1), indicating a diminished influence of QPs in layer M1 — QPs are being trapped in layer M1. This implies that the introduction of a QP trap at the base metal interface (δ∆M1) is a complementary addition to JJ GE (δ∆JJ), and that both are important for suppressing qubit response to impacts from high-energy particles.

This set of measurements was repeated while the accelerator was fired, estimating the qubit frequency once for each 10-measurement series, equivalently once per approximately 85 μs. Resonant pulses were applied with a delay-dependent phase shift resulting in 250 kHz oscillations of the Ramsey signal, which was then fit to recover the frequency shift. Details on the dataset construction, fit procedure, and data quality cuts are presented in Appendix C. We show the resulting frequency shifts in Fig. 6 and elaborate in Appendix C. Consistent with previous work [12, 36] we see that the qubit frequency shifts in response to particle interactions [12]. Unsurprisingly, we also observe that the frequency shift increases with larger energies deposited into the substrate. We note that the frequency shift recovers more quickly for qubits in the JJ&M1 array than for those in the JJ- Only array. Additionally, the frequency shifts of qubits in the JJ-Only array return to their equilibrium values nearly an order of magnitude more slowly than their relaxation rate [Fig. 4(d,h)]. As the qubit frequency shift is a proxy for the QP density near the JJ, this implies that QPs remain near the JJ in the JJ-Only array longer than the JJ&M1 array. Finally, we observe a transient reduction in qubit T2 coinciding with the radiation-induced

These observations lead to two implications. First, QPs can remain near the JJ without causing relaxation or excitation errors. This adds support to the hypothesis that the QP energy distribution is elevated following an radiation impact. Second, the faster recovery time of qubits in the JJ&M1 array implies that a gap difference at the ground-plane/JJ-lead interface δ∆M1 traps QPs away from the JJ, as in Sec. IV B. This reinforces the importance of both δ∆JJ and δ∆M1 for radiation resilience. Further, we observe that for the fast JJ-orientation on the JJ-Only array the frequency shift increases relative to its nominal value, indicating that the QP density actually decreased for a portion of the transient event. This behavior is a physically plausible result of a coupled system of Rothwarf-Taylor style differential equations [Ref. 41 or Sec. V A], with dramatically different effective volumes on either side of the JJ.

3. The dependence of frequency shift measurements on gap profile and JJ orientation. The measured |0⟩ and |1⟩ state probabilities pm 0 (t) and pm 1 (t) are converted into excitation and relaxation transition rates Γ↑(t) and Γ↓(t) by combining our knowledge of the measurement sequences with a “confusion matrix” relating measured and true state probabilities. This process is described in Appendix E

Our model builds on the work in Refs. 11, 42–44. We begin by following Ref. 44 and consider the QP densities in the two metal layers adjacent to the JJ: M2 and M3. To incorporate the gap profile near the JJ, the QP density in layer M2 is broken into two components: x2<

for Eqp < δ∆JJ and x2> for Eqp > δ∆JJ. We add two additional equations to the system presented in Ref. 44 to incorporate the effects of δ∆M1 and the observed orientation dependence. These additions xL and xR model the QP density in layers M1L and M1R (cf., Fig. 1). As in Ref. 44, the base structure of the equations for QP density is in the style of the “Rothwarf-Taylor” phenomenological model describing generation (g), linear trapping (sxi), and quadratic recombination (rx2 i ) [41]:

The QP densities in layer M1 serve as source terms for the QP densities in layers M2 and M3. We assume the QP density in layer M1 behaves independently of the QP population in M2 and M3 due to the volume difference — a QP transitioning between M1 and either M2 or M3 has little effect on the QP densities in the M1. Additionally, the QP densities in layers M2 and M3 are coupled to each other and to qubit transitions. This coupling to qubit transitions allows us to compare the model to the observed excitation and relaxation rates on a perqubit basis. As mentioned in Sec. IV, the “overshoot” behavior is a plausible solution to a coupled system of Rothwarf-Taylor differential equations, though it is not predicted by the specific parameters used in this model. Multiple approximations have been made in this analysis. In terms of the model, physical processes such as QP diffusion are not included. Additionally, the gap engineering parameters used are the nominal, designed values. While these values were extracted from transition temperature measurements on films from the same fabrication process, they were not measured on these individual chips. In terms of data, averaging over accelerator triggers also averages over impacts across the entire qubit substrate. We expect qubits further from the interaction point to exhibit a weaker response [14, 15], and so averaging could smear out this effect and distort our measured qubit responses. Finally, despite our efforts to account for qubit states ≥ |2⟩ through the procedure described in Appendix D 2, the transformation between measured probabilities and transition rates fundamentally assumes a two-level system, which could additionally distort data. Future improvements to this modeling work could be to combine it with radiation and condensed matter simulation packages such as GEANT4 [50] and

ergy depositions from α-particles support a hypothesis that hadronic cosmic rays are a major contributor to the 1 × 10−10 error floor observed in Ref. 1. This is further substantiated by the similarity of the recovery timescale between our work and Ref. 1, and the fact that the correlated error rate observed in Ref. 1 is comparable to the expected impact rate of cosmic rays above 1 MeV [24]. Unlike cosmic ray muons, these hadronic cosmic rays can be mitigated by operation in a shallow (15 m to 30 m) underground facility [25, 31, 38]. While JJ GE is a significant step towards mitigating correlated errors from radiation, additional error mitigation strategies will be required in quantum processors depending on the desired

In addition, α-particles could be expected to become significant in future quantum computers. These highenergy particles can be created by, for example, lightly radioactive components [25] or, as observed in rare-eventsearch particle physics experiments, gaseous radon on surfaces [34, 35, 53]. Should α-particle backgrounds become significant, they can be mitigated by ensuring that materials with line-of-sight to the qubit substrate are radio-pure and radon-free — α-particles have a range of tens of microns in most materials: (approximately 28 μm in silicon and 11 μm in copper at 5.5 MeV [54]). Beyond these high-energy-particle-induced correlated errors, our measurements at CLIQUE show that sub- MeV radiation, such as terrestrial γ-rays and cosmic ray muons, can still cause state transitions in gap-engineered superconducting qubit arrays. The effect of these particles could become apparent as non-radiation sources of error are reduced. While the high rate of these impacts would pose a challenge, the spatial extent of their effect on gap-engineered qubits (and therefore the extent of their effect on QEC) remains unknown. The accelerator data presented here cannot answer these questions as accelerator electron impacts are distributed evenly across the qubit arrays under study, and the data are heavily averaged. These correlations can be studied in detail with a combination of co-located sensors [55] (e.g., microwave kinetic inductance detectors [3], transition-edge sensors [2], or qubits with minimal radiation protection or enhanced radiation sensitivity [56, 57]) and low-energy radiation sources with improved collimation and tagging. Further, this work highlights the importance of understanding radiation’s impact on qubits beyond T1. As previously observed [12, 36], we identify significant qubitfrequency shifts in response to radiation impacts, although they are reduced relative to previous measurements [12]. The reduction with respect to Ref. 12 is likely due to material and gap-engineering differences between measurements. We also identified a transient decrease in qubit T2 following a radiation impact. Additionally, we identify that both the degree of JJ GE (δ∆JJ/hfqb) and the presence of a gap difference at the M1 layer interface (δ∆M1) influence qubit recovery from radiation impacts. While larger δ∆JJ suppresses the initial elevation in qubit transition rate, larger δ∆M1 hastens qubit recovery. The effect of δ∆M1 is most noticeable on the recovery of qubit frequency, where the increased δ∆M1 reduced the recovery times by an order of magnitude. With the knowledge that both δ∆JJ and δ∆M1 influence radiation resistance, future work could focus on maximizing both gap differences and employing other QP-trap and phonon-sink designs [13, 15]. In particular, we highlight a disadvantage of combining highgap base metal with aluminum-based JJs [58, 59] — the negative δ∆M1 turns the JJ into a QP trap, amplifying the impact of radiation and QPs as a whole. As a consequence, this work motivates the pursuit of higher gap JJs (e.g., NbN/AlN and Nb/Al/AlOx) [60–62] and improvements to the film quality of lower-gap base metal materials (e.g., Al, Re, and material stacks utilizing the

Finally, we developed and implemented a timedynamic model of QP density evolution following energy deposition by high-energy radiation. We observed qualitative agreement between this model and our data. This model could serve as the basis for future investigations into how QP and phonon dynamics affect superconducting circuits, and could potentially be incorporated into packages such as G4CMP [51].

Measurements of 241Am utilized sequences A-C. Sequence A always applies a Xπ pulse between qubit measurements. This increases the |1⟩ state population, and enables a measurement primarily sensitive to qubit relaxation. Sequence B never applies a Xπ pulse between measurements. This emphasizes the |0⟩ state population, enabling a measurement primarily sensitive to qubit excitation. Sequence C alternates between A and B on a shot-by-shot basis. This enables near simultaneous measurement of qubit excitation and relaxation. The time between successive qubit measurements in sequences A, B, and C was 6.95 μs for measurements with 241Am. We refer to this time as the “cadence” of the

For measurements carried out at CLIQUE, we added a fourth measurement sequence, D, in addition to sequences A and B. Sequence D performs an “active reset”, using the previous measurement to decide whether or not to apply the Xπ pulse. This sequence was run with the conditional logic targeting either |0⟩ or |1⟩ (D|0⟩ and D|1⟩ respectively). At CLIQUE, sequences A and B had a cadence of 6.55 μs, and sequence D had a cadence of 7.43 μs. We did not use sequence C for measurements at CLIQUE. 2. Appendix B: Alpha Particle Rate Analysis Data Selection The time series shown in Fig. 3(c,d) are an average over multiple radiation impacts identified through the following process. Following data collection, relaxation and excitation errors are computed following the logic described in Sec. III. The response of all qubits is then summed, and then divided by the number of qubits where first measurement was |0⟩ (removing qubits with ambiguous state preparation). This yields a time series dataset of “number of qubit transitions per measurement per valid qubit” — an error probability. This is filtered by cross-correlating with a 100 μs

FIG. 12. Data selection for Fig. 3(c,d). Event shape is estimated by comparing matched filter score and transition probability integral. Events with an integral below a relaxation probability integral of 7.4 (dashed red line) are cut from the analysis. decaying exponential, a “matched filter” [7], to increase the signal-to-noise ratio of radiation impacts. To further improve our sensitivity to radiation impacts we perform a simple event-shape estimation by comparing the peak value found in the matched filter with the integral of the first 15 data points following the matched filter peak. The expectation is that radiation should have an integral that scales more strongly with matched filter height than noise fluctuations. This is what we observe [Fig. 12]. To conservatively select radiation impacts, we remove all events where the integral of the qubit relaxation signal is less than 7.4. 1. Transition Rate Estimation With 241Am Data In the case of the 241Am dataset we do not have sufficient data to constrain the confusion matrix, and therefore rely on Eqns. D6 and D7 to extract the transition rates. We accomplish this by converting our measurements into transition probabilities (described below), and then convert those probabilities into transition rates with Eqns. D6 and D7. The relaxation probability is the probability of |1⟩ transitioning to |0⟩ after 3 μs (the end of the Xπ pulse to the middle of the readout), and the excitation probability is the probability of |0⟩ transitioning to |1⟩ after 6.95 μs (the time between any two subsequent readouts). Once we have extracted Γ↑ and Γ↓, the effective qubit temperature is estimated using Eqn. 6. This process assumes our Xπ fidelity does not change during the interaction. With our Xπ duration of 500 ns the null-to-null spectral width of our pulse is 4 MHz. From Fig. 6 we observe that the qubit frequencies shift less than 100 kHz, therefore we expect the Xπ is largely unaffected by qubit frequency shifts due to radiation.

The goal of the following procedure is to convert the measured state probabilities pm 0 (t) and pm 1 (t) into the qubit excitation and relaxation transition rates Γ↑(t) and Γ↓(t). All told, at any given time point there are four variables that must be solved for: the desired transition rates Γ↑ and Γ↓, and the confusion matrix parameters p00 and p11. The four measurement sequences (A, B, D|0⟩, D|1⟩ in Fig. 2) yield four data points for each time step after the accelerator trigger, enough to constrain these four parameters of interest. To accomplish this, we:

3. Perform least-squares minimization between the predicted and measured ⃗p(t + ∆t). Least-squares minimization was done in Python with iminuit’s migrad algorithm. We observed that in measurements shortly after the radiation impact, approximately the first 50 μs, the converged values of Γ↑, Γ↓, p00, and p11 can take on unphysical values such as transition rates less than zero and probabilities greater than one. Examples of these effects are shown in Figs. 14 and 16. We attribute this to the participation of states ≥ |2⟩, evidenced by deviations from the |0⟩−|1⟩ axis in IQ space, Fig. 18. The participation of these higher states violates the assumption of the two-state measurement sequence model, invalidating the conversion process outlined above. To work around this constraint, we fix p00 and p11 to their values estimated 99.6 ms after a particle interaction. We then obtain Γ↑ and Γ↓ at all time points and use the fit residual (χ2) to quantify the validity of assuming p00 and p11 are constant. In the plots that follow, we cut data points with χ2 > 5.991, a bound which should retain 95 % of data points that follow a χ2 distribution with the expected two degrees of freedom. For completeness, Fig. 16 shows the result of allowing ˆC to vary in the determination of the rates.
